posts.body:
Well, I'm not a specialist with JS/PIXI or WebGL rendering at all, but after some time experimenting with different versions of PIXI, nwjs and so on I concluded that the latest update (not only PIXI, but any kind of software) is not always the best option to pick. Sometimes the older version is better than the most recent.
However I appreciate your effort in writing this guide, but some words of advise, before you post something, make sure it won't cause any trouble, in the case of RPG games, the text is one of the primary factors making the game interesting. I doubt that anyone will try to update PIXI that way if it breaks one of the most important aspects of RPG maker.

Yeah but it is a shame that our dev overlords who own the default rmmz code aren't keeping up to date.
pixi.js came out with v6.5.1 a couple of weeks ago (at time of writing), while the version I think I've got in my project out of the box is v5.2.4, which literally came out in may of 2020.
nw.js came out with v67.1 literally yesterday (at time of writing), while the version I think ships with RMMZ is ... v49? v50? the version that came out coincidentally around the same time as the release used for pixi.js.
These types of version upgrades, while requiring effort to integrate, usually bring some pretty significant performance improvements. While I haven't been successful at upgrading pixi.js because that requires the most effort to update the native code, I have upgraded nw.js without issue and it all by itself is a tremendous upgrade (where I was suffering before).
I commend OP's effort in trying, but this shouldn't be something we have to do. These are dependencies of the product sold by degica and co, and should really be managed by them (or whoever they contract out these efforts to).

A lot of companies are like that unfortunately. If you look at say, Bethesda with their Skyrim and Fallout franchises it was the modders who did a lot of the heavy lifting. It's one of the reasons why I go back to older versions of their games due to the dedicated modders who are innovative and add things that should have been part of the games release.
Worked in IT for years and I'd see companies who only focused on getting the latest and greatest product out (even if it was really only an iteration on previous products.) The budgets would sometimes be huge for development but maintenance budgets to fix bugs, add features were woefully inadequate as they already had the customers money.
Provided support for one financial institution and they had a system that made them millions each year but they still ran it on old hardware and hadn't upgraded the back end application for years. It was so bad that I ended up getting tasked with trying to set up a fix for the underlying service/daemon randomly stopping as the original coders were long gone. It would look like it was still running when it wasn't and their only way of knowing if the app failed was when customers called or someone was actively monitoring. I ended up putting in scripts that would check the state of the service/logs and it would restart it/kill/start depending on the conditions. The developers didn't care because all they were tasked with was keeping the system up and they didn't want to maintain code that been developed 10 years earlier (not that there was a budget for them to do anything on that app.)
Even with DevOps and CI I have seen much the same, the main difference is that there is more of an impetus on F**k it, Ship it as they can have the customers report bugs and fix it later. With the subscription model widely adopted it can be worse - I had subscriptions for products that only had minor updates/fixes where before the previous versions had major updates/changes every 12-18 months.

That being said, I've used some hobby software with even more trash support. First of all, RM is cheap. Dirt cheap. Mixcraft, a hobbiest digital audio workstation, also has a similar price to RM, however doesn't go on sale nearly as often. Their support model I do think is bad; only a few updates on the old spaghetti code of past iterations, then they move on to the next version, where the next version patches software breaking bugs from the previous version but you, the customer, are going to have to pay for the "upgrade" to get those bugs fixed. But hey, they added in a bunch of new features right? Sure, and those are all buggy and won't be fixed until the next version, creating a vicious cycle, except with the feature creep it almost felt like with each version the software became slower and slower.
Honestly, I just assumed all music software was unstable, slow, unoptimized chugging messes until I finally got fed up and moved to Reaper (praise be!) and realized: "Holy , software can be fast AND not crash all the time!?!"
In my opinion, RM gets a lot of support from the devs, and honestly, even without the optimized up-to-date libraries, the software itself runs smoothly and is mostly bug free. Not to mention, anyone is welcome to download the updated libraries and install them themselves (the whole point of this thread, right?) which is pretty nice. A lot of software closes off access to the back-end stuff like that, meaning you're stuck with whatever you get, and if you want updated libraries, tough tits, better pony up the cash for the latest version.

Found the solution to your (and mine) problem.
First, I didn't understand why you moved children from
_windowLayer
to its parent. Imo, it's quite dangerous and unnecessary change. So I skipped applying changes to rpg_scenes.js completely.
Key piece of info to resolve the problem is that webgl renderer became first-class in pixi.js v5. This means that all
_renderWebGL
and
renderWebGL
should be renamed to
_render
and
render
respectively (to be included in rendering process again). Also, I ended up removing most of complex, fragile and now-not-working code and reused original implementations, since it wasn't much relevant to me anyway (masking child mindows based on parent window frame, if I'm not mistaken).
Attached what I've changed migrating Karryn's Prison (original files added, so you can make a diff): pixi4 - before, pixi6 - after.
P.S. If you have
YEP_X_CoreUpdatesOpt.js
plugin, that essentially duplicates s**tload of code from engine while slightly modifying it here and there, you might have to apply all changes to it too. I love Yanfly's code so much...

If you experience performance drops after updating pixijs, check if your GPU supports WebGL (download nw.js
SDK
, press F12 in the game to open devtools, enter
JavaScript:
open('chrome://gpu')
in console)
If you don't see
WebGL: Hardware accelerated
you can:
update you GPU drivers
add parameters
--ignore-gpu-blacklist --ignore-gpu-blocklist
to "chromium-args" in package.json file
However, if slowdown started only after updating nw.js... I won't believe until I see it.
Though you can measure performance in devtools (Performance tab) yourself to see where the bottleneck is
